query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloy protective coatings exhibit superior wear resistance because their near‐equiatomic (uniform) elemental dispersion promotes a consistent lattice distortion that enables the formation of stable, protective oxide phases; these phases (via second-phase strengthening) act as a barrier to wear by enhancing hardness and thermal stability.
generation.material_initial_state: A microwave-cladded Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 high-entropy alloy coating uniformly deposited on SS-304 steel.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled compositional change by shifting from a perfectly equiatomic mix to a non-equiatomic mix (for example, increasing the copper content to 30% while decreasing manganese to 10%) while keeping processing conditions identical.
generation.conditions: Wear testing under identical conditions (e.g., sliding speed of 2 m/s, sliding distance of 1000 m, and a 15 N load), with tests performed at room temperature or under moderate thermal exposure (up to ~800 °C) as typical for these coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of continuous and stable protective oxide phases (e.g., (Fe,Co,Ni,Mn,Cu)3O4 and/or other oxide constituents) arising from uniform lattice distortion and second-phase precipitates.
generation.mechanism: A uniform distribution of the constituent elements creates a homogeneously distorted lattice that favors the nucleation and growth of finely dispersed, protective oxide layers. These oxides, acting as wear barriers, enhance the hardness and thermal stability of the coating, thereby reducing material removal during wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the standard wear test conditions, the equiatomic (Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20) coating will display a lower wear rate (e.g., near the baseline of 0.0018 mm³/m and a stable friction coefficient around 0.2) and a more uniform, continuous protective oxide layer compared to the non-equiatomic (Cu-enriched) variant, which should show increased wear and less consistent oxide formation.
generation.baseline: The established performance of the Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 coating, with measured wear rates around 0.0018 mm³/m and a friction coefficient of 0.2, attributed to its balanced composition and uniform protective phase formation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for coatings produced by methods that ensure a homogeneous elemental distribution (such as microwave cladding) and under wear conditions typical for high-entropy alloy coatings (e.g., moderate load, sliding speeds, and temperatures up to ~800 °C). It may not apply if processing leads to significant segregation or if operating conditions lie far outside the tested regime.
generation.uncertainty: The exact compositional threshold for degradation of the protective oxide layer and the quantitative change in wear rate with non-equiatomic compositions are not fully determined; additional experiments may be needed to map the full parameter space.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings on SS-304 steel using the same processing technique: one set with the equiatomic Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 composition (baseline) and one set with an intentionally skewed composition (for example, Fe20Co20Ni20Cu30Mn10). Subject both sets to identical wear tests (sliding speed ~2 m/s, load 15 N, sliding distance 1000 m) and conduct detailed microstructural and phase analyses (using SEM, XRD) on the worn surfaces to assess oxide layer formation.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during the test
SEM images to evaluate the continuity of protective oxide layers
XRD phase identification of oxide constituents
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the non-equiatomic (Cu-enriched) coatings exhibit wear rates and oxide layer continuity equal to or better than those of the equiatomic baseline, the hypothesis that uniform elemental dispersion is key to superior wear resistance through protective oxide formation would be falsified.
